title: Journey to the Centre of the Earth
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The deepest hole that humans have ever drilled, on the Kola Peninsula in Russia, is just over twelve kilometres deep. That sounds impressive, but it is less than two-tenths of one per cent of the distance to the centre of the Earth, which is about 6,370 kilometres. Scientists cannot therefore examine the interior directly, and they have learned about it mostly from the waves produced by earthquakes, which travel through the planet and change speed and direction when they meet different materials. From this evidence they have concluded that the Earth is made of four main layers.

The outermost layer is the crust, a thin shell of rock on which we live. Beneath the oceans it is only about seven kilometres thick, and beneath the continents it averages about thirty-five kilometres, though it can reach seventy kilometres under high mountains. If the Earth were an apple, the crust would be no thicker than the skin. It is broken into huge slabs, called tectonic plates, which move very slowly, at about the speed at which fingernails grow, and this movement is the cause of earthquakes and volcanoes.

Beneath the crust lies the mantle, which is by far the thickest layer. It extends to a depth of about 2,900 kilometres and makes up about eighty-four per cent of the Earth's volume. The mantle is made of hot, dense rock. It is not liquid, but over millions of years it flows very slowly, like extremely thick toffee, carrying heat from the interior towards the surface. The temperature rises from about 1,000 degrees Celsius at the top to more than 3,500 degrees at the bottom.

Below the mantle is the outer core, a layer of liquid metal about 2,200 kilometres thick, made mainly of iron with some nickel. Its temperature is between 4,000 and 5,000 degrees Celsius. The liquid moves in great swirling currents, and because the metal conducts electricity, these movements create the Earth's magnetic field. This field extends far into space and protects the planet from harmful particles from the Sun. Without it, the atmosphere might have been stripped away long ago.

At the centre is the inner core, a ball of solid iron and nickel about 1,220 kilometres in radius, which is roughly three-quarters the size of the Moon. It is as hot as the surface of the Sun, about 5,500 degrees Celsius, but it stays solid because the pressure there, more than three million times that of the atmosphere at sea level, prevents the metal from melting. The inner core is growing very slowly as the Earth cools, by about a millimetre a year.

How do we know all this? When an earthquake occurs, it sends out two kinds of waves. P-waves, which are like sound, can pass through both solids and liquids, but S-waves, which shake the rock from side to side, cannot cross a liquid. In 1906, the Irish geologist Richard Oldham noticed that S-waves did not arrive on the far side of the Earth, and he concluded that part of the interior must be liquid. Three decades later, the Danish scientist Inge Lehmann used the paths of P-waves to show that inside the liquid core there is a smaller solid one.

Understanding the interior is more than a matter of curiosity. The mantle's slow movement explains why continents drift, why mountains rise and why some regions suffer earthquakes and others do not. The core's magnetic field has reversed direction many times in the planet's history, and it is now weakening in some regions, which worries engineers who depend on satellites. Dr Yusuf Demir, a geophysicist, says that every new measurement of the deep Earth is likely to bring surprises, because the planet is far more active than it appears from the surface.
